input: Write a one-minute elevator pitch for my startup

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: A one-minute pitch can focus on different things — problem/solution, traction, team, vision — knowing what must be covered versus left out shapes the entire structure.
The pitch must be tuned to its audience — an investor wants ROI and market size, a potential customer wants benefits, a partner wants synergy — the same startup needs a very different pitch for each.
Where and how this will be delivered (in-person networking event, a cold email, a video, a competition) changes the tone, pacing, and whether a call-to-action is needed.
One minute is the stated limit, but knowing if there is a strict word count, a formal format requirement, or a submission deadline affects how tightly the copy must be written.
The founder's personal voice and desired tone — bold and punchy vs. thoughtful and data-driven — determines the style of language used throughout the pitch.
Knowing what specific action or reaction the pitch should trigger (book a follow-up meeting, remember the brand, sign up for a demo) lets the pitch be built backwards from that outcome.
Understanding the startup's core product, the problem it solves, and any existing pitch material is the baseline content needed before writing a single word.

gold.taskTitle: Write a one-minute elevator pitch for startup
gold.taskDescription: Draft a spoken, one-minute elevator pitch that clearly and compellingly communicates the startup's value to a target listener.

questions.title: What does your startup do and what problem does it solve?
questions.description: Capture the core product or service and the specific pain point it addresses — the essential raw material for the pitch.

questions.title: Who is the primary audience for this pitch?
questions.description: Identify whether the pitch is aimed at investors, potential customers, strategic partners, or another group, so the framing and emphasis can be tailored accordingly.

questions.title: Where and how will this pitch be delivered?
questions.description: Determine the delivery format — live networking event, pitch competition, video recording, cold email — as this shapes tone, pacing, and structure.

questions.title: What one thing should the listener do after hearing it?
questions.description: Pin down the single desired outcome — book a call, visit a website, invest, sign up — so the pitch can be built backwards from that call-to-action.

questions.title: What must the pitch include versus what can be left out?
questions.description: Clarify whether specific elements like traction data, team credentials, market size, or a demo offer are required or optional, to avoid a pitch that tries to cover everything.

questions.title: What tone and style best represents your founder voice?
questions.description: Establish whether the pitch should feel bold and punchy, warm and story-driven, or precise and data-backed, so it sounds authentically like the founder.

questions.title: Is there a strict word count or format requirement to meet?
questions.description: Find out if there are hard constraints such as a competition's submission rules, a time limit enforced by a timer, or a slide format that the pitch must conform to.
